# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. The series argues for universal background checks (UBC) and an assault weapons ban (AWB); copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and year. Population and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Headline toll: total gun deaths (CDC). Breakdowns by intent go in the appendix.
B3. Children and teens: "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; give the age range in the appendix.
B4. Background checks: use the Miller, Hepburn & Azrael (2017) estimate (22%).
B5. Mass shootings: GVA counts; GVA's definition in the appendix.
B6. Rifle share of homicides: if it comes up, one sentence, then mass-casualty lethality.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

 Assault weapon platform lethality in US mass public shootings 1966–2025

 Abstract
 Firearm violence is a leading cause of premature death worldwide, and mass public shootings sit at the far tail of severity. Research has linked higher casualty counts to assault weapons, but the category enters those studies as a single yes/no indicator, so the weapon characteristics behind the association remain unidentified. We analyzed 197 US mass public shootings from 1966 through 2025 (202 perpetrators, 433 firearms, 288 fired) recorded in The Violence Project Mass Shooter Database, splitting the assault weapon category into weapon platforms, cartridge energy classes, and magazine capacity. Assault weapon use held between 17 and 20% of incidents per decade from the 1970s through the 2000s, then rose to 36% in the 2010s and 60% in the incomplete 2020s, with the shift concentrated after 2015. In adjusted negative binomial models, assault weapon use was associated with 55% more fatalities and roughly four times as many injuries; excluding the 2017 Las Vegas shooting cut the injury estimate to 2.3. The AR-15 was the only platform associated with both outcomes, but an additive model of platform and cartridge is rejected in favor of an interaction (likelihood ratio P < .05 for both outcomes, with and without the Las Vegas outlier), and neither component carries the association alone. Excluding Las Vegas and adjusting for magazine capacity, incidents in which an AR-15 fired a rifle-class cartridge had 1.6 times the fatalities and 2.4 times the injuries of the reference category, while rifle-class cartridges fired from other platforms showed none. Large-capacity magazines were independently associated with both outcomes, at 1.4 for fatalities and 1.8 for injuries, and the magazine estimate for fatalities moved little across every model we fit. What the binary classification records as one exposure is a compound of platform, ammunition, and magazine capacity, and the components do not behave alike.

 By John Gramlich 

 Around 44,000 people died of gun-related injuries in the United States in 2024, according to the latest available statistics from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The number of gun deaths fell for the third consecutive year but was still among the highest annual totals on record.

 Here are answers to some common questions about gun deaths in the U.S., based on a Pew Research Center analysis of data from the CDC, the FBI and other sources. You can also read our public opinion findings about U.S. gun violence and gun policy.

 About this research 
 This Pew Research Center analysis answers common questions about gun deaths in the United States. It looks at how the number and rate of these deaths have changed over time and how the U.S. compares with other countries and territories on these metrics, among other topics.

 Why did we do this? 

 Pew Research Center does research to help the public, media and decision-makers understand important topics. This analysis builds on our previous work about guns and gun policy in the U.S.

 How did we do this? 

 We relied primarily on mortality data collected by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and published in its WONDER database . Our analysis includes supplemental data from the FBI’s Crime Data Explorer , as well as cross-national statistics from the Global Burden of Disease database published by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington. Additional information about all sources can be found by following the links in the text.

 In 2024, the most recent year with complete data, 44,447 people died from gun-related injuries, according to the CDC. That figure includes gun homicides and gun suicides, along with three less common types of gun-related deaths the CDC tracks: those that involved law enforcement, those that were accidental and those with undetermined circumstances.

 The total excludes deaths in which gunshot injuries played a contributing, but not principal, role. (CDC fatality statistics are based on information from official death certificates, which identify a single cause of death.)

 Though they tend to get less public attention than gun-related homicides, suicides have long accounted for the majority of U.S. gun deaths . In 2024, 62% of all gun-related deaths in the U.S. were suicides (27,593), while 35% were homicides (15,364). The rest involved law enforcement (636), were accidental (450) or had undetermined circumstances (404); each of these categories accounted for around 1% of all gun deaths, according to CDC data.

 What share of  all  homicides and suicides in the U.S. involve a gun?

 In 2024, 76% of all U.S. homicides (15,364 of 20,162) involved a firearm. That was down a bit from other recent years, but still among the highest percentages since 1968 – the earliest year for which the CDC has online records.

 In addition, 57% of all suicides in 2024 (27,593 of 48,824) involved a gun. That was higher than in recent years, but below the peak of 61% in both 1993 and 1990.

 Key takeaways:

 Firearm deaths dropped from 2023 to 2024, mostly due to a 15.8% drop in firearm homicides.

 But firearm suicides reached an all-time high, while gun mortality remains an issue in several demographics.

 Firearm deaths decreased by 5% from 2023 to 2024 in the U.S., although such mortalities remain high, with one occurring every 12 minutes, a report from the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions shows.

 Rose Kim, MPA , an assistant policy advisor at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told Healio that the decrease is encouraging but “nearly 45,000 Americans died of firearm injuries, which was the fifth highest total ever recorded. While overall firearm deaths and firearm homicides have decreased since 2021, overall firearm deaths remain well above pre-pandemic levels due to the increase in firearm suicides.

 Data derived from press release.

 “What’s noteworthy is that firearm suicides have reached an all-time high in the total number of deaths for the fourth consecutive year,” she added. “In 2024, nearly two-thirds of all firearm deaths were suicides, meaning America’s firearm mortality crisis is increasingly a suicide crisis .”

 In the latest edition of Johns Hopkins’ annual report on firearm mortality, Kim and colleagues found that guns were involved in 44,447 deaths in 2024, with the decrease “largely due to a 15.8% drop in the homicide rate, with 15,364 homicides in 2024,” according to a press release.

 The decrease in firearm homicides “demonstrates that investments in evidence-based prevention policies can make a significant difference,” Kim said. “Communities should build on and not retreat from successful prevention strategies.”

 The report, which utilized CDC death-certificate data on several categories of firearm deaths, also showed that about 86% of total gun deaths were men.

 The total firearm mortalities in 2024 are down from 48,830 in 2021 — a drop of around 9% — when gun violence peaked “amid the social disruption of the COVID-19 pandemic, and have been decreasing slowly since then,” the release said.

 But firearm homicides have continued to jump up in certain demographics over the last decade. For example, such deaths rose by 63%, 39% and 31% among Black women, Asian or Pacific Islander women, and Hispanic/Latino women, respectively, from 2015 to 2024, while white women experienced a 2% rise during that time.

 Black women (169%), Asian or Pacific Islander women (51%) and Hispanic/Latino women (57%) also experienced major rises in gun suicides from 2015 to 2024.

 Meanwhile, for the fifth consecutive year, gun violence remained the leading cause of death among youth aged 1 to 17 years in 2024, with 2,214 total gun deaths.

 The researchers also found that firearm suicides totaled 27,593 deaths last year, up from 27,300 in 2023 and a new record-high for the fourth straight year .

 Kim told Healio this number aligns with increased gun ownership rates beginning in 2020.

 “As a result, more people are increasingly exposed to firearms, and many firearm-owning households with children continue to leave at least one gun unlocked and/or loaded, making firearms easily accessible and available,” she said. “Access to lethal means, like firearms, greatly increases the risk that a suicide attempt will result in death as firearms are the most lethal suicide method.”

 According to Kim, clinicians should ask all patients about firearm ownership and be given information about safe and secure practices for firearm storage “regardless of risk level.”

 “Patients with an elevated risk for firearm injury should receive lethal means counseling, which is a voluntary, patient-centered health care intervention by helping at-risk patients and their families reduce access to lethal means,” she said. “Through lethal means counseling training, clinicians can be formally trained on how to speak to their patients about firearm safety practices.”

 Kim also advised that clinicians utilize safety planning , “an evidence-based and effective technique to reduce suicide risk, to guide their patients to identify effective coping techniques to use during crises. Safety plans should be personalized to each patient and be developed collaboratively with each patient and family. Developing a safety plan in advance can help patients and their families prepare to get through crises.”

 92 Days in Gun Violence 

 By the Numbers: Gun Violence in Q4 2025

 Our quarterly analysis from the Gun Violence Data Hub dives into the latest trends.

 By Aaron Mendelson 

 Jan 13, 2026 

 Erik Carter for The Trace 

 The Trace 

 Go beyond the headlines.

 Your weekly briefing on gun violence.

 Email Address 

 The Weekly Briefing

 The Trajectory

 The Bulletin

 Data Hub

 Events

 Subscribe

 Copy link 

 Share on Facebook 

 Email a link to this page 

 Welcome to 92 Days In Gun Violence, a quarterly update from The Trace’s Gun Violence Data Hub. In this edition, we’re tracking trends from the fourth quarter of 2025 in near-real-time (or as close as the data allows).

 The Q4 dispatch features updates on noteworthy data, Data Hub collaborations, and academic research from the past quarter. Additional information on the year in gun violence is available in The Trace’s 2025 roundup .

 Shooting Numbers Continue to Plunge

 The U.S. experienced 14,655 shooting deaths in 2025, according to data from the Gun Violence Archive (GVA).

 The deadliest day of the year for gun violence was January 1, 2025, with 90 shooting deaths. No fewer than 19 people were shot and killed each day in the United States. (One of those least deadly days was in Q4, on November 24).

 But, on the whole, the news was positive: In 2025, the U.S. recorded the fewest shooting deaths of any year since 2015. Controlling for population brings the picture into even clearer focus. The rate of shooting deaths in the U.S. last year was 4.3 per 100,000 residents. That’s the lowest number the GVA has recorded in over a decade.

 Zeroing in on just the fourth quarter, another positive trend appears. Looking only at October, November, and December, the data shows that 2025 had fewer shooting deaths and injuries than any other year during Q4. GVA’s data goes back to 2014, so that means it was the lowest Q4 figure in at least 11 years.

 In addition to the deaths, shootings caused 26,238 nonfatal injuries in 2025, according to GVA’s data, the lowest raw total since 2014.

 There are important caveats here — GVA does not capture every shooting. GVA can enter or update data on shootings weeks or months after they happen. (These numbers were pulled from GVA on January 6.) It also does not track gun suicides. Still, this is the best and most timely information available.

 The data also reveals widespread declines in shootings at the state level. Just eight states saw an increase in gun deaths last year, while 41 recorded a decline (as did Washington, D.C.; Delaware’s number was flat).

 Gun Sales Dip

 14.7 million guns were sold in the U.S. in 2025, according to our tracker . The final quarter of 2025 showed a continued dip in sales, with the lowest Q4 total (4.4 million) since 2019.

 The numbers are estimates calculated by The Trace using FBI data — you can read more about the process here . Yearly sales were down about 4 percent from 2024, and considerably down from the pandemic gun-buying boom. Many dealers believe the president’s gun-friendly policies have put a damper on their sales . The yearly total includes 8.9 million handguns and 5.8 million long guns.

 The trends in individual states are more varied. Six states had an increase of 2 percent or greater in gun sales: Nevada, Rhode Island, New York, Washington, Iowa, and Georgia. Colorado, which posted an increase in sales through three quarters after the passage of a suite of gun-related bills, finished the year with a slight dip in sales compared to 2024.

 Thirty-two states posted a decline in gun sales of 2 percent or more, as did Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico. The states that saw the biggest declines were Michigan, Massachusetts, Alabama, Oregon, and New Hampshire.

 Mass Shootings

 GVA recorded 408 mass shootings in the U.S. in 2025. They resulted in 395 deaths and 1,867 injuries.

 Mass shootings in the last quarter included a shooting at a child’s birthday party in Stockton, California, that killed four people, three of them children, and a shooting at Brown University that killed two students and injured nine more. The death toll for Q4 mass shootings was 113, down from 181 the year before.

 GVA’s definition of mass shootings is wider than some: “a minimum of four victims shot, either injured or killed, not including any shooter who may also have been killed or injured in the incident.”

 While mass shootings attract significant media attention, the data shows the daily drip of gun violence is a far bigger killer. Mass shootings accounted for just 2.7 percent of shooting deaths tracked by GVA in 2025.

 One New Thing: Shootings During Immigration Raids

 The Trace has been tracking incidents in which federal agents shot someone or held them at gunpoint during an immigration enforcement action under Trump’s crackdown. As of January 12, we’ve identified 16 incidents in which immigration agents shot someone and another 15 incidents in which agents held someone at gunpoint. This includes the shooting of a 37 year-old woman in Minneapolis last week .

 We’ve also identified another 13 incidents in which immigration agents fired less-lethal munitions, like rubber bullets and pepper balls, at suspects or members of the public.

 The Gun Violence Data Hub also published or updated eight datasets during Q4 2025; you can find those in our Data Library . Users can also head over to The Trace’s Atlas of American Gun Violence to explore GVA data on shootings from Q4 2025 in an interactive map.

 Partnership Spotlight: Local Coverage of Gun Suicides Among Those Over 70

 Our dataset and national story on gun suicide among older Americans — a growing trend that hits rural white men especially hard — has resulted in collaborations with newsrooms in over a dozen states.

 The most recent of these was published by CalMatters in late December . It’s a deeply reported and sobering look at how “rural Northern California counties have some of the nation’s highest rates of gun suicides among older adults.” The rate in rural California counties is more than triple that of its urban areas.

 The story has been picked up by news outlets from Redding to San Francisco to Santa Barbara .

 Academic Spotlight: Housing Discrimination and Gun Violence

 A group of Tufts University School of Medicine researchers recently examined the relationship between historical redlining in mortgage lending and current-day shootings. They found a significant relationship between the two, writing that their findings “suggest that coordinated housing and firearm policy reforms may mitigate enduring disparities.” The research is featured in the December 2025 Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities .

{"content": "# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
Northgate Progress Institute, Washington, D.C.
Safer Communities series. Publication date: October 27, 2026. Draft for editorial review.

### Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 44,447 Americans in 2024, one death every 12 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fifth consecutive year (CDC final mortality data, released February 2026).
- Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years obtained it without a background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, 2017), and only 19 states and the District of Columbia require checks on all gun sales (RAND, 2025).
- Assault weapons were used in 60% of mass public shootings so far this decade, up from roughly one in five through the 2000s, and attacks with them produce 55% more fatalities per incident (Densley and Peterson, 2026). Congress should close both gaps in the next session.

### 1. The toll

In 2024, 44,447 people in the United States died by gun violence, according to final data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is one death every 12 minutes, around the clock, all year. It is the fifth-highest annual total ever recorded in this country, and as in every year since 1995, more than half of those deaths were suicides (appendix table A2).

The number is falling, and that matters. Gun deaths have declined for three consecutive years from the 2021 peak of 48,830, and the gun homicide rate fell 15.8% between 2023 and 2024. Declines of that size do not happen on their own. They follow policy, investment and enforcement in the states and cities that have pursued them. Three good years are an argument for more of the same, not less. A country that can cut its gun death toll by 9% in three years has no basis for accepting 44,000 deaths a year as the price of doing business.

What has not moved is the age of the victims.

### 2. Children and teens

Guns killed 2,214 children and teens between the ages of 1 and 17 in 2024, according to the CDC data analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions. For the fifth consecutive year, firearms killed more young people than any other single cause, including car crashes, overdoses and cancers.

The toll is not evenly distributed by age: 1,547 of those deaths were among 15- to 17-year-olds, and 450 among children aged 10 to 14. But no age group is untouched. Ninety-eight children between the ages of 5 and 9 were killed by gunfire in a single year, and 119 were between 1 and 4 years old.

That is the figure that should discipline this debate. When the leading cause of death for American children and teens is a consumer product that Congress has the power to regulate, the question is not whether to act but which interventions will reach the fewest mistakes to the fewest families.

### 3. The background-check gap

Federal law has required a background check on every gun purchased from a licensed dealer since the Brady Act took effect in 1994. It has never required one on a private sale, whether that sale happens online, at a kitchen table or in the parking lot of a gun show. In most of the country, a person barred from buying a gun at a licensed counter can legally buy one an hour later from an unlicensed seller.

The scale of that gap is well measured. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired their most recent firearm within the previous two years obtained it without a background check, according to the peer-reviewed national survey by Miller, Hepburn and Azrael published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2017. Among private sales, those made other than through a store or pawnshop, half of firearms changed hands with no check at all.

The system itself is not the problem. Since 1994 the National Instant Criminal Background Check System has blocked more than 4 million sales to prohibited purchasers, among them convicted felons and people subject to domestic violence restraining orders. Background checks work every time they are actually required.

The problem is where they are not required. Nineteen states and the District of Columbia have closed the gap with their own comprehensive background check laws, according to RAND's Gun Policy in America analysis as of January 2025. Thirty-one states have not, and a prohibited purchaser in those states can simply route around the states that have. This is also the rare policy question on which the country has already reached agreement: nearly 85% of gun owners support universal background checks, according to a December 2024 survey of 5,100 gun-owning registered voters by 97Percent.

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive recorded 407 mass shootings in the United States in 2025, four or more people shot in a single incident, excluding the shooter. Even in the lowest year since before the pandemic, that is more than one mass shooting every day, killing 395 people and injuring 1,867 more.

The weapons used in these attacks have changed. A September 2026 study in Scientific Reports analyzed 197 mass public shootings from 1966 through 2025 recorded in the Violence Project Mass Shooter Database. Assault weapons were used in 17% to 20% of incidents per decade through the 2000s, then 36% of incidents in the 2010s and 60% so far in the 2020s. The same study found that attacks involving assault weapons produced 55% more fatalities and roughly four times as many injuries as attacks with other firearms, and that large-capacity magazines independently raised fatalities by 40%.

Rifles of all types still account for a small share of American murders overall, 401 of the 15,795 murders reported to the FBI in 2024, but that is the wrong denominator for this question. The case for restricting assault weapons is about casualty counts per attack, and that is precisely where the shift has occurred.

There is also direct evidence on the policy. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting deaths from 1981 to 2017 found that the risk of dying in a mass shooting was 70% lower during the years the federal assault weapons ban was in force than in the periods before and after it. That ban took effect in 1994 and, because Congress wrote it with a 10-year sunset, expired in September 2004. Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston all happened after it lapsed, and all were carried out with weapons the 1994 law would have prohibited from new manufacture.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer in every state, licensed or private, online and at gun shows, with no carve-outs that let prohibited purchasers route around the states that have already acted. Twenty-two percent of recent acquisitions without a check is a national standard written in preventable deaths.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 prohibition and modernize it: cover the AR-15 platform and its copies, ban large-capacity magazines alongside the rifles, and this time do not grandfather the existing stock, which is what blunted the effect of the original law.

3. **Fund the research.** Sustain and expand the federal gun violence prevention research program at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health. Congress first restored dedicated funding in fiscal 2020 at $25 million a year, after more than two decades in which the federal government studied the country's second-leading cause of death for young people barely at all.

4. **Incentivize state extreme risk laws.** Create grant funding for states to enact and implement extreme risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis, and for the training that makes them usable. Connecticut's law was associated with a 13.7% reduction in firearm suicides, and Indiana's with a 7.5% reduction, with no evidence of harm to lawful gun owners.

The tools are tested, the evidence is public and the support is bipartisan outside Washington. What is missing is a Congress willing to use them.

---

*Sources for every figure in this brief are listed in the accompanying data appendix. Statistics are drawn from the most recent finalized federal data available as of the October 2026 copy deadline.*

{"content": "# NPI fact sheet: Gun safety policy by the numbers

**Closing the gaps: Universal background checks and an assault weapons ban**
Northgate Progress Institute | Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | October 27, 2026 | For use by Hill offices

---

**44,447 Americans died by gun violence in 2024.** One death every 12 minutes, the fifth-highest annual total ever recorded.
*Source: CDC Underlying Cause of Death, final 2024 data, released February 2026.*

**2,214 children and teens ages 1-17 died by gunfire in 2024.** Guns were the leading cause of death for this age group for the fifth consecutive year, killing more young people than car crashes, overdoses or cancers.
*Source: CDC final 2024 data, analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions.*

**22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years got it without a background check.** Among private sales, those made outside a store or pawnshop, the share with no check at all was 50%.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
Northgate Progress Institute, Washington, D.C.
Safer Communities series. Publication date: October 27, 2026. Draft for editorial review.

### Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 44,447 Americans in 2024, one death every 12 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fifth consecutive year (CDC final mortality data, released February 2026).
- Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years obtained it without a background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, 2017), and only 19 states and the District of Columbia require checks on all gun sales (RAND, 2025).
- Assault weapons were used in 60% of mass public shootings so far this decade, up from roughly one in five through the 2000s, and attacks with them produce 55% more fatalities per incident (Densley and Peterson, 2026). Congress should close both gaps in the next session.

### 1. The toll

In 2024, 44,447 people in the United States died by gun violence, according to final data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is one death every 12 minutes, around the clock, all year. It is the fifth-highest annual total ever recorded in this country, and as in every year since 1995, more than half of those deaths were suicides (appendix table A2).

The number is falling, and that matters. Gun deaths have declined for three consecutive years from the 2021 peak of 48,830, and the gun homicide rate fell 15.8% between 2023 and 2024. Declines of that size do not happen on their own. They follow policy, investment and enforcement in the states and cities that have pursued them. Three good years are an argument for more of the same, not less. A country that can cut its gun death toll by 9% in three years has no basis for accepting 44,000 deaths a year as the price of doing business.

What has not moved is the age of the victims.

### 2. Children and teens

Guns killed 2,214 children and teens between the ages of 1 and 17 in 2024, according to the CDC data analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions. For the fifth consecutive year, firearms killed more young people than any other single cause, including car crashes, overdoses and cancers.

The toll is not evenly distributed by age: 1,547 of those deaths were among 15- to 17-year-olds, and 450 among children aged 10 to 14. But no age group is untouched. Ninety-eight children between the ages of 5 and 9 were killed by gunfire in a single year, and 119 were between 1 and 4 years old.

That is the figure that should discipline this debate. When the leading cause of death for American children and teens is a consumer product that Congress has the power to regulate, the question is not whether to act but which interventions will reach the fewest mistakes to the fewest families.

### 3. The background-check gap

Federal law has required a background check on every gun purchased from a licensed dealer since the Brady Act took effect in 1994. It has never required one on a private sale, whether that sale happens online, at a kitchen table or in the parking lot of a gun show. In most of the country, a person barred from buying a gun at a licensed counter can legally buy one an hour later from an unlicensed seller.

The scale of that gap is well measured. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired their most recent firearm within the previous two years obtained it without a background check, according to the peer-reviewed national survey by Miller, Hepburn and Azrael published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2017. Among private sales, those made other than through a store or pawnshop, half of firearms changed hands with no check at all.

The system itself is not the problem. Since 1994 the National Instant Criminal Background Check System has blocked more than 4 million sales to prohibited purchasers, among them convicted felons and people subject to domestic violence restraining orders. Background checks work every time they are actually required.

The problem is where they are not required. Nineteen states and the District of Columbia have closed the gap with their own comprehensive background check laws, according to RAND's Gun Policy in America analysis as of January 2025. Thirty-one states have not, and a prohibited purchaser in those states can simply route around the states that have. This is also the rare policy question on which the country has already reached agreement: nearly 85% of gun owners support universal background checks, according to a December 2024 survey of 5,100 gun-owning registered voters by 97Percent.

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive recorded 407 mass shootings in the United States in 2025, four or more people shot in a single incident, excluding the shooter. Even in the lowest year since before the pandemic, that is more than one mass shooting every day, killing 395 people and injuring 1,867 more.

The weapons used in these attacks have changed. A September 2026 study in Scientific Reports analyzed 197 mass public shootings from 1966 through 2025 recorded in the Violence Project Mass Shooter Database. Assault weapons were used in 17% to 20% of incidents per decade through the 2000s, then 36% of incidents in the 2010s and 60% so far in the 2020s. The same study found that attacks involving assault weapons produced 55% more fatalities and roughly four times as many injuries as attacks with other firearms, and that large-capacity magazines independently raised fatalities by 40%.

Rifles of all types still account for a small share of American murders overall, 401 of the 15,795 murders reported to the FBI in 2024, but that is the wrong denominator for this question. The case for restricting assault weapons is about casualty counts per attack, and that is precisely where the shift has occurred.

There is also direct evidence on the policy. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting deaths from 1981 to 2017 (DiMaggio et al., 2019) found that the risk of dying in a mass shooting was 70% lower during the years the federal assault weapons ban was in force than in the periods before and after it. That ban took effect in 1994 and, because Congress wrote it with a 10-year sunset, expired in September 2004. Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston all happened after it lapsed, and all were carried out with weapons the 1994 law would have prohibited from new manufacture.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer in every state, licensed or private, online and at gun shows, with no carve-outs that let prohibited purchasers route around the states that have already acted. Twenty-two percent of recent acquisitions without a check is a national standard written in preventable deaths.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 prohibition and modernize it: cover the AR-15 platform and its copies, ban large-capacity magazines alongside the rifles, and this time do not grandfather the existing stock, which is what blunted the effect of the original law.

3. **Fund the research.** Sustain and expand the federal gun violence prevention research program at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health. Congress first restored dedicated funding in fiscal 2020 at $25 million a year, after more than two decades in which the federal government studied the country's second-leading cause of death for young people barely at all.

4. **Incentivize state extreme risk laws.** Create grant funding for states to enact and implement extreme risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis, and for the training that makes them usable. Connecticut's law was associated with a 13.7% reduction in firearm suicides and Indiana's with a 7.5% reduction (Kivisto and Phalen, 2018), with no evidence of harm to lawful gun owners.

The tools are tested, the evidence is public and the support is bipartisan outside Washington. What is missing is a Congress willing to use them.

---

*Sources for every figure in this brief are listed in the accompanying data appendix. Statistics are drawn from the most recent finalized federal data available as of the October 2026 copy deadline.*

**Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban**
Northgate Progress Institute | Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Publication date: October 27, 2026. Draft for editorial review.

Source line format follows the NPI style sheet: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL. All figures in the brief appear below, one table per figure. Statistics are drawn from the most recent finalized federal data available at the October 2026 copy deadline.

---

## Table A1. Total gun deaths in the United States, 2021-2024

| Year | Total gun deaths | Firearm suicides | Firearm homicides | Other |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2021 | 48,830 | 26,328 | 20,958 | 1,544 |
| 2022 | 48,204 | 27,032 | 19,651 | 1,521 |
| 2023 | 46,728 | 27,300 | 17,927 | 1,501 |
| 2024 | 44,447 | 27,593 | 15,364 | 1,490 |

Notes: "Other" is the residual and combines legal intervention (636 in 2024), unintentional discharge (450 in 2024) and undetermined intent (404 in 2024). 2024 is the fifth-highest annual total ever recorded and the third consecutive annual decline, a cumulative drop of about 9% from the 2021 peak. The firearm homicide rate fell 15.8% between 2023 and 2024. One gun death occurred every 12 minutes on average in 2024. The series is based on death certificate data from the CDC Underlying Cause of Death database; 2024 final data were released in February 2026.

Source: Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, The Firearm Mortality Epidemic: Examining the U.S. Data from 2024, July 2026, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/data/annual-gun-violence-data
Source: Pew Research Center, What the Data Says About Gun Deaths in the U.S., April 28, 2026, https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/28/what-the-data-says-about-gun-deaths-in-the-us/

## Table A2. Gun deaths by intent, 2024

| Intent | Deaths | Share of all gun deaths |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suicide | 27,593 | 62% |
| Homicide | 15,364 | 35% |
| Legal intervention | 636 | 1% |
| Unintentional | 450 | 1% |
| Undetermined | 404 | 1% |
| **Total** | **44,447** | **100%** |

Notes: Suicides have been the majority of U.S. gun deaths every year since 1995. The 2024 suicide total is the highest ever recorded and the fourth consecutive record year. Firearms were used in 57% of all U.S. suicides and 76% of all U.S. homicides in 2024. About 86% of gun deaths in 2024 were men.

Source: Pew Research Center, What the Data Says About Gun Deaths in the U.S., April 28, 2026, https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/28/what-the-data-says-about-gun-deaths-in-the-us/

## Table A3. Gun deaths among children and teens, ages 1-17, 2024

| Age group | Gun deaths |
| --- | --- |
| 1-4 | 119 |
| 5-9 | 98 |
| 10-14 | 450 |

# NPI fact sheet: Gun safety policy by the numbers

**Closing the gaps: Universal background checks and an assault weapons ban**
Northgate Progress Institute | Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | October 27, 2026 | For use by Hill offices

---

**44,447 Americans died by gun violence in 2024.** One death every 12 minutes, the fifth-highest annual total ever recorded.
*Source: CDC Underlying Cause of Death, final 2024 data, released February 2026.*

**2,214 children and teens ages 1-17 died by gunfire in 2024.** Guns were the leading cause of death for this age group for the fifth consecutive year, killing more young people than car crashes, overdoses or cancers.
*Source: CDC final 2024 data, analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions.*

**22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years got it without a background check.** Among private sales, those made outside a store or pawnshop, the share with no check at all was 50%.
*Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017.*

**Only 19 states and the District of Columbia require background checks on all gun sales.** In the other 31 states, a person prohibited from buying at a licensed dealer can legally buy from an unlicensed seller.
*Source: RAND, Gun Policy in America, as of January 1, 2025.*

**Background checks have blocked more than 4 million sales to prohibited purchasers since 1994.** The system works every time it is actually required.
*Source: National Instant Criminal Background Check System data compiled by Everytown for Gun Safety, 2022.*

**407 mass shootings in the United States in 2025.** More than one a day, every day, even in the lowest year since before the pandemic. They killed 395 people and injured 1,867.
*Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2025.*

**Assault weapons were used in 60% of mass public shootings so far this decade.** Up from 17% to 20% per decade through the 2000s. Attacks with assault weapons produced 55% more fatalities and roughly four times as many injuries.
*Source: Densley and Peterson, Scientific Reports, September 2026.*

**Nearly 85% of gun owners support universal background checks.** There is no constituency for the loophole except the people it protects.
*Source: 97Percent 2024 Gun Owner Survey of 5,100 gun-owning registered voters.*

---

**What Congress should do:** pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, sustain federal gun violence research funding at the CDC and NIH, and fund state extreme risk laws.

**Full sourcing and methodology:** see the data appendix to Safer Communities Brief No. 9.

# Social cards: Safer Communities Brief No. 9

Northgate Progress Institute | Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Publication date: October 27, 2026. Draft for editorial review. Four cards, one per pillar of the brief: the toll, children and teens, background checks, assault weapons.

---

## Card 1: The toll

**One American killed by a gun every 12 minutes.**

44,447 gun deaths in 2024, the fifth-highest annual total ever recorded.

Source: CDC Underlying Cause of Death, final 2024 data.

## Card 2: Children and teens

**Guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens.**

Fifth consecutive year. 2,214 young people ages 1-17 killed in 2024.

Source: CDC final 2024 data, Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions.

## Card 3: Background checks

**1 in 5 recent gun buyers faced no background check.**

Half of all private gun sales involved no check at all.

Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017.

## Card 4: Assault weapons

**Assault weapons now used in 6 in 10 mass public shootings.**

Attacks with them cause 55% more deaths and four times the injuries.

Source: Densley and Peterson, Scientific Reports, 2026.

---

## Production notes

Design: NPI teal #0F6E6E background with white type, coral #E4572E for the headline stat, per style sheet section B7. Cards carry the brief title and the NPI wordmark; no charted axes are used at this size.

Alternate lines held in reserve if the editor wants to swap a card:
- 407 mass shootings in 2025, more than one a day. Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2025.
- Only 19 states require background checks on all gun sales. Source: RAND, 2025.

Full source lines in the format required by style sheet section C1 are in the data appendix, tables A1, A3, A4 and A6.
All five deliverables are complete. Let me flag the key editorial decisions to the Director of Publications before submitting.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9

## Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention**
Northgate Progress Institute, Washington, D.C.
Safer Communities series. Publication date: October 27, 2026. Draft for editorial review.

### Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 44,447 Americans in 2024, one death every 12 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fifth consecutive year (CDC final mortality data, released February 2026).
- Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years obtained it without a background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, 2017), and only 19 states and the District of Columbia require checks on all gun sales (RAND, 2025).
- Assault weapons were used in 60% of mass public shootings so far this decade, up from roughly one in five through the 2000s, and attacks with them produce 55% more fatalities per incident (Densley and Peterson, 2026). Congress should close both gaps in the next session.

### 1. The toll

In 2024, 44,447 people in the United States died by gun violence, according to final data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is one death every 12 minutes, around the clock, all year. It is the fifth-highest annual total ever recorded in this country, and as in every year since 1995, more than half of those deaths were suicides (appendix table A2).

The number is falling, and that matters. Gun deaths have declined for three consecutive years from the 2021 peak of 48,830, and the gun homicide rate fell 15.8% between 2023 and 2024. Declines of that size do not happen on their own. They follow policy, investment and enforcement in the states and cities that have pursued them. Three good years are an argument for more of the same, not less. A country that can cut its gun death toll by 9% in three years has no basis for accepting 44,000 deaths a year as the price of doing business.

What has not moved is the age of the victims.

### 2. Children and teens

Guns killed 2,214 children and teens between the ages of 1 and 17 in 2024, according to the CDC data analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions. For the fifth consecutive year, firearms killed more young people than any other single cause, including car crashes, overdoses and cancers.

The toll is not evenly distributed by age: 1,547 of those deaths were among 15- to 17-year-olds, and 450 among children aged 10 to 14. But no age group is untouched. Ninety-eight children between the ages of 5 and 9 were killed by gunfire in a single year, and 119 were between 1 and 4 years old.

That toll should discipline this debate. When the leading cause of death for American children and teens is a consumer product that Congress has the power to regulate, the question is not whether to act but how fast.

### 3. The background-check gap

Federal law has required a background check on every gun purchased from a licensed dealer since the Brady Act took effect in 1994. It has never required one on a private sale, whether that sale happens online, at a kitchen table or in the parking lot of a gun show. In most of the country, a person barred from buying a gun at a licensed counter can legally buy one an hour later from an unlicensed seller.

The scale of that gap is well measured. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired their most recent firearm within the previous two years obtained it without a background check, according to the peer-reviewed national survey by Miller, Hepburn and Azrael published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2017. Among private sales, those made other than through a store or pawnshop, half of firearms changed hands with no check at all.

The system itself is not the problem. Since 1994 the National Instant Criminal Background Check System has blocked more than 4 million sales to prohibited purchasers, among them convicted felons and people subject to domestic violence restraining orders. Background checks work every time they are actually required.

The problem is where they are not required. Nineteen states and the District of Columbia have closed the gap with their own comprehensive background check laws, according to RAND's Gun Policy in America analysis as of January 2025. Thirty-one states have not, and a prohibited purchaser in those states can simply route around the states that have. This is also the rare policy question on which the country has already reached agreement: nearly 85% of gun owners support universal background checks, according to a December 2024 survey of 5,100 gun-owning registered voters by 97Percent.

### 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive recorded 407 mass shootings in the United States in 2025, four or more people shot in a single incident, excluding the shooter. Even in the lowest year since before the pandemic, that is more than one mass shooting every day, killing 395 people and injuring 1,867 more.

The weapons used in these attacks have changed. A September 2026 study in Scientific Reports by Densley and Peterson, who built and maintain the Violence Project Mass Shooter Database, analyzed 197 mass public shootings from 1966 through 2025. Assault weapons were used in 17% to 20% of incidents per decade through the 2000s, then 36% of incidents in the 2010s and 60% so far in the 2020s. The same study found that attacks involving assault weapons produced 55% more fatalities and roughly four times as many injuries as attacks with other firearms, and that large-capacity magazines independently raised fatalities by 40%.

Rifles of all types still account for a small share of American murders overall, 401 of the 15,795 murders reported to the FBI in 2024, but that is the wrong denominator for this question. The case for restricting assault weapons is about casualty counts per attack, and that is precisely where the shift has occurred.

There is also direct evidence on the policy. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass shooting deaths from 1981 to 2017 (DiMaggio et al., 2019) found that the risk of dying in a mass shooting was 70% lower during the years the federal assault weapons ban was in force than in the periods before and after it. That ban took effect in 1994 and, because Congress wrote it with a 10-year sunset, expired in September 2004. Uvalde in 2022, Parkland in 2018 and Lewiston in 2023 all happened after the ban lapsed, and all were carried out with weapons and magazines the 1994 law would have prohibited from new manufacture.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer in every state, licensed or private, online and at gun shows, with no carve-outs that let prohibited purchasers route around the states that have already acted. A 22% no-check rate is not a loophole. It is a national standard written in preventable deaths.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 prohibition and modernize it: cover the AR-15 platform and its copies, ban large-capacity magazines alongside the rifles, and this time do not grandfather the existing stock, which is what blunted the effect of the original law.

3. **Fund the research.** Sustain and expand the federal gun violence prevention research program at the CDC and the National Institutes of Health. Congress first restored dedicated funding in fiscal 2020 at $25 million a year, after more than two decades in which the federal government studied the leading cause of death for American children and teens barely at all.

4. **Incentivize state extreme risk laws.** Create grant funding for states to enact and implement extreme risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from a person in crisis, and for the training that makes them usable. Connecticut's law was associated with a 13.7% reduction in firearm suicides and Indiana's with a 7.5% reduction (Kivisto and Phalen, 2018), with no evidence of harm to lawful gun owners.

The tools are tested, the evidence is public and the support is bipartisan outside Washington. What is missing is a Congress willing to use them.

---

*Sources for every figure in this brief are listed in the accompanying data appendix. Statistics are drawn from the most recent finalized federal data available as of the October 2026 copy deadline.*

**44,447 Americans died by gun violence in 2024.** One death every 12 minutes, the fifth-highest annual total ever recorded.
*Source: CDC Underlying Cause of Death, final 2024 data, released February 2026.*

**2,214 children and teens ages 1-17 died by gunfire in 2024.** Guns were the leading cause of death for this age group for the fifth consecutive year, killing more young people than car crashes, overdoses or cancers.
*Source: CDC final 2024 data, analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions.*

**22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years got it without a background check.** Among private sales, those made outside a store or pawnshop, the share with no check at all was 50%.
*Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017.*

**Only 19 states and the District of Columbia require background checks on all gun sales.** In the other 31 states, a person prohibited from buying at a licensed dealer can legally buy from an unlicensed seller.
*Source: RAND, Gun Policy in America, as of January 1, 2025.*

**Background checks have blocked more than 4 million sales to prohibited purchasers since 1994.** The system works every time it is actually required.
*Source: National Instant Criminal Background Check System data compiled by Everytown for Gun Safety, 2022.*

**407 mass shootings in the United States in 2025.** More than one a day, every day, even in the lowest year since before the pandemic. They killed 395 people and injured 1,867.
*Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2025.*

**Assault weapons were used in 60% of mass public shootings so far this decade.** Up from 17% to 20% per decade through the 2000s. Attacks with assault weapons produced 55% more fatalities and roughly four times as many injuries.
*Source: Densley and Peterson, Scientific Reports, September 2026.*

**Nearly 85% of gun owners support universal background checks.** There is no constituency for the loophole except the people it protects.
*Source: 97Percent 2024 Gun Owner Survey of 5,100 gun-owning registered voters.*

---

**What Congress should do:** pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, sustain federal gun violence research funding at the CDC and NIH, and fund state extreme risk laws.

**Full sourcing and methodology:** see the data appendix to Safer Communities Brief No. 9.

# New NPI brief: Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban would close the gaps that cost American lives

**WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026.** Gun violence killed 44,447 Americans in 2024, one every 12 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fifth consecutive year, according to a brief released today by the Northgate Progress Institute.

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the Gaps," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention, argues that the gaps Congress has refused to close are measurable in lives. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years obtained it without a background check, and half of all private sales involved no check at all (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, 2017). Only 19 states and the District of Columbia require checks on all gun sales (RAND, 2025).

The weapons are also changing. Assault weapons were used in 60% of mass public shootings so far this decade, up from roughly one in five through the 2000s, and attacks with them produce 55% more fatalities and about four times as many injuries (Densley and Peterson, 2026).

"Every one of these numbers is a family," Dr. Whitfield said. "We are not short of evidence and we are not short of public support. Nearly 85% of gun owners back universal background checks. What we are short of is a Congress willing to act on what it already knows. Three straight years of falling gun deaths show prevention works when we fund it and apply it. It is time to apply it everywhere."

The brief calls on Congress to pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004 without grandfathering the existing stock, sustain federal gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and fund state extreme risk laws.
